body: Allowing the `button` element to navigate on its own seems rather unsafe from an XSS perspective. The set of elements that can navigate has been stable for a long time.

Hi Anne, I really appreciate the quick reply!

Why is the following, proposed HTML

```html
<button action="/new" method="POST">New</button>
```

any more insecure, from an XSS perspective, than this currently-supported HTML?

```html
<form action="/new" method="POST">
  <button>New</button>
</form>
```

As you said, the set of elements that can trigger navigations has been stable for a long time. This includes buttons! From a web user perspective, nothing has changed—users can and already do expect that clicking a button could lead them to a new page.

From an HTML author perspective, both `action` and `method` are brand new attributes, so there shouldn't be any existing buttons that are dynamically populating these attribute values for which this change would introduce new XSS vulnerabilities. It could introduce a new XSS vulnerability if website authors were allowing user-generated input to set attributes names *and* values for existing buttons, like so:

```html
<button ${unescapedUserInput}>New</button>
```

However, this practice is already unsafe and vulnerable to XSS, as it allows for `$[unescapedUserInput}` to be an inline script, `form`, or `formaction`, or `formmethod`, attribute, so I don't see how the addition of an `action` or `method` attribute to the button would introduce a new surface area for XSS. Happy to be proven wrong though, and would certainly support a mechanism to mitigate this if necessary.

Hey Oliver, thanks for mentioning the [Sanitizer API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTML_Sanitizer_API) and including such a precise example. It was really helpful to play around with and this is exactly the kind of scrutiny I want this proposal to receive.

To create this hypothetical vulnerability, the following things have to be true somewhere out there in the world:

1. The web author is deliberately choosing to set HTML based on untrusted input (rather than escaping it all)
2. They are allowing a subset of elements for their specific UX
3. They have chosen to allow `<button>`s to render
4. They have chosen to _deny-list_ known unsafe attributes (but with a sanitizer that still removes `on*` attributes)

The first two are reasonable and common. Letterboxd, for example, lets you write movie reviews with [a subset of HTML tags for formatting](https://letterboxd.com/about/faq/#review-formatting). An important use-case to cover.

The third step is questionable. As reflected by Sanitizer API's choice to [block buttons by default](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTML_Sanitizer_API/Default_sanitizer_configuration), it's clearly inadvisable to let users specify actual buttons. I struggle to think of any situation in which I, as the builder of a web platform, want to allow HTML-specified UGC (user-generated content), let that UGC specify buttons that look like real site controls, but also have those buttons do nothing. I'm sure such a thing exists somewhere, but it's clearly inadvisable and not something that any sanitizer tool would let you do unintentionally.

The fourth step is where I think it becomes highly implausible. Now the hypothetical web author has not only made the affirmative choice to allow UGC buttons, but they have chosen to remove attributes from buttons, specifically, via a deny-list. An allow-list would make some sense, because you could choose to allow `class` or `style`, I suppose (it's still a bad idea, but sure). A deny-list is far more error-prone. There are so many XSS-unsafe attributes that you are virtually bound to forget one, so you're going to rely on the sanitizer having a pre-existing deny-list of bad attributes that will still get removed even though you didn't explicitly specify them.

Therefore, the hypothetical web author who would be made-newly vulnerable by this feature is extremely informed about XSS dangers, is using a sophisticated sanitizer to allow certain elements and attributes, and wants to allow-by-default every attribute on a button except the (manually-specified) attributes that can alter the URL and HTTP method of a form and the (not manually-specified) event handler attributes.

Not only does this extant vulnerability require a high degree of (seemingly) implausible intent, it also requires a specific API that is not widespread in HTML sanitizers: a deny-list feature for attributes with a list of attributes that will still get removed even if they are excluded from the deny-list. It exists in the new web Sanitizer API, as well the sanitization library used in in [Ruby on Rails](https://github.com/rails/rails-html-sanitizer#railshtmltargetscrubber). The latter also has a [safelist](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/blob/c895c8b2ac9c7255ca10c4e3083b8f0b019b7189/lib/loofah/html5/safelist.rb) that allows the `href`, `action`, and `method` attributes (Unlike the Sanitizer API, it also allows buttons and forms by default.) However, the [OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer](https://github.com/OWASP/java-html-sanitizer) has a custom policy `disallowAttributes` method that simply [reverses an existing `allow`](https://www.javadoc.io/doc/com.googlecode.owasp-java-html-sanitizer/owasp-java-html-sanitizer/20240325.1/org/owasp/html/HtmlPolicyBuilder.html#disallowAttributes(java.lang.String...)) and [html-sanitize](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/97e9d56df10bf95217bc5e50e60301ec4d37e923/packages/sanitize-html/README.md#L4) (the most-popular HTML santizer on NPM) doesn't seem to have an comporable interface at all. 

Personally I'd argue that `action`, `method`, `formaction`, and `formmethod` should get added to that automatic exclusion list, since they can also control HTTP requests. Fortunately, if the standards committee sees it the same way, that's something we can correct in the Sanitizer API, since it's also in the web platform. (And on the flip side: if they don't see it as an XSS-vulnerability candidate on a form, why would it be one on a button?)

I know that the web operates at an immense scale that makes [Murphy's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murphy%27s_law) close to a reality. We can explore alternatives with worse APIs that wouldn't have this specific issue. But to Anne's point: the elements that can navigate on their own have been stable for a very long time. It seems to me that the safest way to implement this feature is to leverage that history—I'm more than happy to evangelize improvements to important sanitizer libraries, for instance, but most the ones I've seen so far _already_ make this configuration close to impossible, precisely because of that history. (OWASP, html-sanitize, and the Sanitize API all disallow buttons from the default policies, for example; I'm going to add a more complete survey of libraries to the proposal document). If there's a possibility this proposal is not forward compatible with the security profile of existing websites, we should be able to surface evidence of that.

`formaction` was originally named `action` but it the name needed to be changed due to web compat.

As far as I can tell, the requested functionality already exists with the `form`, `formaction` and `formmethod` attributes. It's just that a `form` element is required, and forms can't be nested.

As @annevk said, this would introduce a new way to cause a navigation. Developer convenience is not sufficient benefit to introduce a security-sensitive feature that also has known web compat issues.

@zcorpan would you be willing to re-open the issue? I understand that it's not currently planned—that's why I'm proposing it. I would appreciate the opportunity to address yours and others' concerns. The discussion has been productive so far.

> formaction was originally named action but it the name needed to be changed due to web compat.

Could you please share what the compat issues are, and some links to old discussions if you have them? `formaction` is the right name for that feature, because it edits the form's `action`; I'm trying to give the button its _own_ action. We could use a different name if there are compat concerns, but I chose `action` because it fits perfectly with the existing grammar.

> As far as I can tell, the requested functionality already exists with the `form`, `formaction` and `formmethod` attributes. It's just that a form element is required, and forms can't be nested.

The requested functionality does not currently exist because, as you noted, [you cannot describe actions inside a form that don't submit the form content](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#form-wrapper-workaround). The proposal contains a detailed example of a common ["edit draft" UX](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#multi-action-pages) whose implementation goes from being impossible to trivial.

> Developer convenience is not sufficient benefit to introduce a security-sensitive feature that also has known web compat issues.

Noting that there _are_ common patterns that are impossible without this feature, I also want to push back on "developer convenience" as a useful prioritization framing. If something is inconvenient to do in HTML, web authors will do the convenient thing at the expense of security, accessibility, and correctness; this proposal aims to end the endless saga of [pre-fetching logout links](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#link-button-workaround), which persists (I believe) because the "right" solution is harder than the wrong one. The HTML standard is a powerful tool for encouraging best practices by making them the most convenient ones.

I understand it's security-sensitive and I would love to hear more about what those specific concerns are so that we can explore mitigations to ameliorate them!

Hi @alexpetros 

What if instead of new `action`/`method` attributes on `<button>`, we reserved something like `_self` as a magic value for the existing `form=` attribute — similar to how `target=` already has `_self`, `_blank`, `_top`, `_parent` as reserved values?

```html
<button form="_self" formaction="/logout" formmethod="post">Logout</button>
```

The browser would implicitly associate the button with a virtual self-form. No new attributes, no new navigation surface - just a reserved token on an attribute that already handles exactly this kind of association.

This addresses most of the concerns raised here:

- **Web compat**: zero new attribute names, so the `formaction`-was-renamed-from-`action` issue doesn't apply
- **Sanitizers**: nothing new to deny/allow-list - `form=`, `formaction=`, and `formmethod=` are already known quantities
- **Navigation surface**: buttons already navigate via `form=` association today, this just makes the form implicit

### The polyfill argument

The thing that convinced me this is the right shape for the feature is that a complete polyfill already works in every shipped browser right now:

```html
<form id="_self"></form>  <!-- placed at top of body -->

<button form="_self" formaction="/logout" formmethod="post">Logout</button>
```

The only limitation is that submit events fire on the `<form>` rather than the `<button>`, which matters if you're hooking JS listeners — but for the core use case of simple no-JS buttons this is fine, and authors who want it today don't have to wait.

The fact that this polyfill works means `form="_self"` isn't really introducing a new capability to the web platform - it's formalizing a pattern that already exists, with the exact same security profile browsers already accept.

### On the XSS surface

I did think carefully about whether `form="_self"` genuinely expands the attack surface. There is one edge case worth naming: in a shadow root or iframe, `form=` id lookup is scoped to that boundary, so a sanitizer that blocks `<form>` but allows `formaction`/`formmethod` buttons is currently accidentally safe - no form exists in scope for the button to attach to. `form="_self"` with an implicit virtual form would remove that accidental safety net.

But honestly I think this is a pretty theoretical concern. A sanitizer in that configuration is already broken in the regular DOM, where an attacker can just reference any existing form id on the page. The shadow root case is only "safe" by coincidence, not by design. Any sanitizer serious enough to be reasoning about this attack surface should be using an allowlist, in which case `formaction` wouldn't be permitted in the first place. If this was a real concern blocking _self lookups in shadow roots would be possible I guess.

So I don't think this proposal should be held to a higher bar than the status quo it builds on - especially when the polyfill demonstrates that browsers already consider this behavior acceptable today.

Hi
I'm using dummy forms (empty of <input>s) outside the main form for submit buttons other than POST method. Something like this
```
<form id=main action="/resource">
  <input type=text name=field1/>
  <input type=text name=field2/>
  <input type=text name=field3/>
  <button formmethod=POST>SAVE</button>
  <button formmethod=POST name=method realmethod=PUT formaction="/resource/_id_">UPDATE</button>

  <button formmethod=POST name=method realmethod=DELETE form=dummyDelete formaction="/resource/_id_">DELETE</button>
  <button formmethod=GET form=dummyGet formaction="/resource/childResourceList">LIST CHILD</button>
  <button formmethod=GET form=dummyNavigation formaction="/navigateSomewhere">GO SOMEWHERE</button>
</form>
<form id=dummyDelete></form>
<form id=dummyGet></form>
<form id=dummyNavigation></form>
```
It's not the best solution, forms without semantics (#12330) and not a proper way to express the methods desired (#3577).
I support both #12330 and #3577

Another note is that unlike the current proposal https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions adjusting the handling of form attribute semantics on buttons instead of adding a new action attribute to buttons would likely also mean we would have to expand the scope to include 
```html
<input type="submit" form="_self" formaction="/logout" formmethod="post" value="Logout">
```
As currently submit inputs are just buttons and already are navigation triggering elements just like buttons in current browser design so if we address buttons we likely have to think about both.  

The other thing to note is that inputs and buttons with values that submit with _self would likely have to also submit their value via url parameters or body formData which likely matches the current browser spec and implementation anyway

Anyway not sure if this new idea fits in this closed issue or deserves a new Issue for the change in scope.

@MichaelWest22's option is a genius compromise but it does have some drawbacks. In addition to being much more verbose, `formaction` is a confusing name for that attribute, because no form is involved. To the extent that forms are involved, they expand the surface the area of the change, raising weird questions like [what to do with `<input type=button>`](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12330#issuecomment-4676129936), which he identifies above. Lastly, the form polyfill and  @lcchueri's dummy form workaround have a downside identified [in the proposal](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#form-wrapper-workaround): a trailing, empty `?` query string.

I really appreciate @lcchueri's [dummy form example](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12330#issuecomment-4672523287) because it shows why the current semantics make it prohibitively complex to model even a very simple set of controls in HTML. It's extremely difficult to tell what controls correspond to the actual form and which ones correspond to all the fake forms required to make the buttons do anything. Having to write a separate, detached, `<form>` element for every `<button>` that doesn't submit a form—often quite far away, because nesting is illegal—is a highly error-prone and confusing, which makes JavaScript is near-mandatory to do anything with buttons beyond "logout." 

JavaScript implementations of basic features are not just less accessible than declarative ones, they also make it less likely that authors will adopt other good security features. Now that the website depends on a lot of JavaScript, there's a good chance that JavaScript was written with in that would make a strict CSP effortful to implement (i.e. with `<script>` tags); an HTML implementation of this page, however, could trivially adopt a very strict CSP. This is one of many ways in the inconvenience of accomplishing basic tasks in HTML makes the median website overall less secure.

It doesn't have to be this way! With this proposal and [proper method support](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3577), the entire form can be written very simply, resulting in a UX that is far more accessible and secure than if the latter three buttons had to be enabled with JavaScript.

```html
<form id=main action="/resource">
  <input type=text name=field1/>
  <input type=text name=field2/>
  <input type=text name=field3/>
  <button formmethod=POST>SAVE</button>
  <button formmethod=PUT formaction="/resource/_id_">UPDATE</button>

  <button method=DELETE action="/resource/_id_">DELETE</button>
  <button action="/resource/childResourceList">LIST CHILD</button>
  <button action="/navigateSomewhere">GO SOMEWHERE</button>
</form>
```

I think Micheal's workaround is a decent option if the concerns about extant sanitization of buttons are completely un-resolvable to standards committee's satisfaction. I won't rehash my [earlier comments](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12330#issuecomment-4641586315) on that issue, but I think they can be resolved, and I will do some additional research on existing sanitizer APIs as well.

> I suppose the concern is that web developers have written sanitizer code in the past with certain assumptions in mind.

The last two decades of web security have shown over and over again that blacklists don't work for sanitizing. As such, I have a difficult time understanding what assumptions you think are invalided that are not already broken by design.

Hi everyone! I can't thank you all enough for participating in this issue. It makes the proposal a lot stronger and a lot likelier to happen.

A lot of the feedback that I've received revolves around the difference between buttons and links i.e. why use a button when links can do navigation. I'm working on updating the proposal with an in-depth examination of the semantic and behavioral differences between buttons and links. I think that will help guide a lot of the discussion and also illustrate the importance of the proposal. Once it's done I will share and summarize it here. (Hopefully this takes me no more than a week or two.)

@matthewquinn, to your second question, I was just translating @lcchueri's form verbatim to illustrate how the proposal simplifies it. I have a [similar, but simpler, example](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#multi-action-pages), referenced earlier, that replicates a common "drafting" or "editing" experience. You are given the option to post your draft, save your draft, or discard your edits. I have exactly that set of buttons in the webview of my email provider, for instance.

> I have also been in situations where form nesting felt like the right thing to do

To be clear, nesting forms is the status quo—I'm trying to remove the need for nesting forms by giving buttons the ability to act independently. 

From a user's perspective, both "cancel" and "save" are sibling actions on the same context; it's only because buttons can't make independent navigations that web authors are given a suboptimal choice: either style a "cancel" link as button and try to make it behave like one, or use an event listener to make the "cancel" button trigger a navigation. Both of these require JavaScript and both have drawbacks that can be avoided by adopting this proposal.

I've updated [the proposal](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions) based on everyone's excellent feedback. The new material is [Sections 5-7](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#buttons-vs-links). A few highlights that address comments in this thread:

[Section 5](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#buttons-vs-links) explains the semantic differences between buttons and links, raised by a few commenters. **Links represent a destination that can be opened in many contexts; buttons represent an action that only makes sense in the current context.** Buttons already have the ability to navigate, they just lack the ability to navigate to a subset of URLs. This creates significant demand for ["link buttons"](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#link-buttons) that visually communicate button semantics (which is correct) but are forced to rely on the actual functionality and semantics of a link (which is incorrect), a pattern with [un-resolvable UX and accessibility problems](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#link-button-accessibility). 

This section should also answer the suggestion from @theodoreb. I think the introduction of a `method` attribute to links is a bad idea. Not only are links (ideally) always safe requests, they inherently offer the user the ability to re-contextualize them. It would be extremely confusing if links suddenly had to guard against being copied without their non-GET method.

[Section 6](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#existing-workarounds) addresses the existing workarounds. [Form wrappers](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#form-wrapper-workaround) don't work for GET requests and cannot be used in nested contexts for POST requests. [Dangling forms](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#dangling-forms) can be used as a workaround for POST requests in nested contexts, but this creates a significant surface area for XSS, as the introduction of a new form element can hijack the functionality of an otherwise-trusted button; dangling forms are also prohibitively complex and don't scale for any real-world usage (which is why no documentation recommends you use forms that way and almost no one does).

[Section 7.2](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#self-buttons) addresses the `form="_self"` workaround proposed by @MichaelWest22. Unfortunately, I don't think this is worth it. This proposal seeks to provide safe and secure patterns that can displace incorrect and inaccessible HTML usage on the web. Even if browsers were to implement a special case that removes the query parameter for `form="_self"`, the result is still a syntax that is technical, confusing, and unlikely to be adopted by the stakeholders who need it most. The wrong thing would still be easier and look more correct than the right thing.

[Section 7.3](https://triptychproject.org/proposals/button-actions#Use-a%20different%20name%20besides%20) provides workarounds for the web compact concerns mentioned by @zcorpan. I think `href` and `url` are both compelling alternatives to `action`. Even `location` could work. What's important is that it's a name that correctly communicates what the attribute does (i.e. no `form*` semantics)

I'm currently working on an analysis of the all major HTML sanitizers to determine whether any of them have APIs that would be risked by the introduction of a new `action` or `href` attribute to the `<button>` element. It's just going to take a little bit of work, and I wanted to get the other additions out there so people can comment on them. Thanks for the engagement so far!

The proposal here identifies real issues that are encountered every day in building applications with HTML. I personally work with (and on) Django, but it's framework independent. (Inter alia) Both the multi-action pages examples and the buttons vs links discussion from the proposal describe almost canonical problems. 
 
The Django Steering Council supports this proposal. It would enable simpler patterns that will help us write better markup.
